So how could the whole internet really go away? Realistically, there is one way. The Sun.
In September eighteen fifty-nine, a giant storm from the Sun hit Earth. Telegraph lines across North America failed.
In Pittsburgh, a manager reported streams of fire from the circuits. In Washington, an operator was badly shocked, and paper caught fire.
In Boston, operators unplugged their batteries and still sent messages to Portland, Maine. They used only the current from the northern lights. The sky was the power supply.
The lights were seen as far south as Cuba.
In July twenty twelve, a storm just as strong erupted from the Sun and missed Earth.
The space physicist Daniel Baker said it was at least as strong as the one in eighteen fifty-nine. The only difference, he said, is that it missed.
A study by the National Academy of Sciences put the total cost of such a storm at more than two trillion dollars.
And power would be the bigger problem: NASA notes that multi-ton transformers damaged by a storm like that might take years to repair.
Scientists estimate the chance of one hitting Earth is between one point six and twelve percent per decade. That is a single estimate, not a forecast.
Here is the twist. In twenty twenty-one, the computer scientist Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi asked what such a storm would do to the internet.
The fibre itself is immune. But long cables have repeaters every fifty to a hundred and fifty kilometres to boost the signal, powered along a wire.
Those repeaters are vulnerable to induced currents.
GPS and communication satellites are directly exposed to a storm too, and could lose connectivity during it.
Her paper warns of outages that could cover the entire globe and last several months.
Submarine cables are at greater risk than land cables, and the United States is at higher risk of disconnection than Asia.
